questions.evidence:
For a classroom observation, students place one drop of colored water on each of three surfaces: plain paper, waxed paper, and a plastic lid. They use the same dropper and try to make every drop the same size. A timer starts after each drop lands.

On plain paper, the wet mark spreads and becomes wider. On the other two surfaces, the water stays gathered into a small rounded drop during the observation period. Students sketch the shape at ten seconds and again at one minute.

Eva says that the plain paper must be weaker because its mark is larger. Her partner points out that the activity records how water behaves on a surface, not how much weight a material can hold. A spreading mark does not directly measure strength.

They decide to title the page Water on Three Surfaces and keep any strength question for a separate investigation. The pictures are useful because the students explain what was compared and when each observation was made.
questions.explanation: 活動記錄十秒及一分鐘的水形。
options: The maximum weight each surface can hold.
The price of making every material.
The shape of water on each surface at two specified times.
The lifetime of all paper products.

questions.evidence: They decide to title the page Water on Three Surfaces and keep any strength question for a separate investigation. The pictures are useful because the students explain what was compared and when each observation was made.
questions.explanation: 標題應準確反映已測內容，不加入未測強度。
options: It says all three drops behaved identically.
It hides the surface names from readers.
It proves which material is strongest.
It names the observed relationship without adding an untested claim.
questions.prompt: Why does the chosen title fit better?
